ergo: The way to put an end to

Not so. The familiarity with vio-
lence breeds carelessness of blood-

of life does not prevent the illegal
murders that fill the columns of our
daily journals. Few murderers care
for the hereafter. It is the present
that concerns them. Imprisonment
for life, the pardoning power taken
out of the hands of the executive, certain conviction for the crime, as far
as human effort could convict, and
certain punishment for conviction,
these might avail. Certain it is that
the multiplication of hangings does
not decrease the commission of mur-
ders in the localities where such hang-
ings occur. The records of the courts
show this and beyond this the LIGHT
did not assert. The way to end mur-
ders is to instruct and civilize, and
Judicial hangings only serve to horrify

and defeat their own intention. To

be more thoroughly and unmistak-
ably defined and no legal subterfuges
permitted to prevent conviction. Be-
cause hanging familiarizes with vio-
lence and does not restrain from mur-
der it does not follow that no punish-
ment at all would operate as a deter-
rent. The estimate of the value of
human life is too low now, and that
estimate is not raised by hanging.

A thin woman in blue glasses had been obliged to bestow herself on the driver's seat, and back to back with her sat a stout woman with swapping black eyes and big bundle on her lap that looked as if it might contain somebody's linen.

A passenger wanted to get off and gave the usual signal. The black-eyed woman caught it a second sooner than the conductor, and before he could raise his whistle to his lips she shot her umbrella over the back of her seat and with its iron-shod tip gave the driver a vigorous prod right in the middle of his spinal column. The woman in blue glasses reinforced it with a robust twitch at the tail of his coat, and the conductor, seeing by this time that he wasn't in it, withheld the customary whistle. The driver brought his horses up standing, and with rather a scared face turned round and asked what's the matter. The woman in blue glasses informed him in matter-of-course way, as if the whole proceeding had been strictly according to routine, that passenger wanted to get off.

The driver "held his horses" in more senses than one while the passenger descended and until he had started up his steeds again; then he turned around and proceeded to restore discipline in his end of the car.

"Madam," he said, with fine sarcasm, to the woman in blue glasses, "you might noticed we carry a conductor on this car. See him up there at the other end of it? H. E. Bidwells zeal for God and man
will not let him rest quietly under the
EAGLES dictum forbidding theological
arguments in its columns. One can feel
that he is full of his subject, but the
EAGLES restraining talon holds him in
check. Therefore, he quietly hay-presses
his thoughts and slips in as matter OF
private information ten line receipt,
warranted to knock Ingersolism in the
head, prove Gods existence, and set
Christ right before the people.


He casts his thought in the form of
two crisp sentences, not verse nor stanza
and what is more remarkable, not
scripture-but all out of his own head.
It is not my intention to add or de-
tract, or, such is my reverence for pro-
fnndity of thought, even to repeat AIr.
Bidwell's two sockdologers; but all good
men should refer to the EAGLES last
Sunday edition and secure clipping for
hat FASTING.


And thus, let it be hoped, his thought
will permeate to posterity, filter through
our ritualistic literature, and finally rest
endiademed in our Holy Writ.


Yours truly,


g. L. LEWISTON.
Wichita, July 90, 1891.

RICHMOND, Va. June 9, 1891.
To the Editor of the Dispatch:

In reference to the article in last Sunday's DISPATCH on the subject of "Lightning and Cars," notice that in an interview Mr. H. W. Wells states that "the system of lightning-arresters and protectors is almost perfect, and lines well constructed and supplied with such devices are not liable to accidents on account of storms." As this statement might lead the public to consider that this company is careless of their interests in the matter of reliable street-car service, and also that we recklessly expose our property to damage which might easily be prevented, we think it only right that we should present our views on the subject.

We admit with Mr. Wells that the system of lightning is "almost perfect," but we state positively that no arrester on the market to-day will afford absolute protection from damage by lightning to street-car machinery, where the earth is used as "a part of the electrical circuit." The arresters we have in use we consider as good as any yet made. They are, however, of the class described by Mr. Wells as almost perfect—that is, they fail sometimes. Regarding the recent stoppage of cars during storms, what stated to your reporter was that whilst we had so much machinery damaged by lightning we would not consider it prudent to risk further damage, which might incur serious inconvenience to the public, but that when repairs were completed we would again run, storm or no storm.

I am asked to name one place where it is customary to stop operations during storm. I could name several, but I mention here the case of the Southside Railway Company, of Manchester, Va.

Their road is equipped with one of the latest style lightning-arresters manufactured by the same company with which Mr. Wells' employers are associated. Their experience is that twice within one week they lost their machinery from lightning, causing a stoppage of their road on one occasion for half day and on the other for several days. They don't trust their almost perfect lightning-arrester now, but promptly shut off current during storm.

Yours truly, J. W. LaFFORD,
Superintendent Light Department,
Richmond Railway and Electric Company.

The celebrated Guelph fund which cablegrams have referred was created in 1865 in fulfillment of an agreement between King William and the dethroned King George of Hanover, by which the latter was to receive an indemnity of 16,000,000 talers for the loss of his sovereign rights, the capital to be held in trust by the Prussian Government and the interest to be paid in perpetuity to the heirs of the Brunswick-Luneburg family. Bismarck encountered strong opposition from the Liberals, who objected not only on account of the massive sum but because the deposed king had not formally abdicated. By entering into the agreement brought about through the mediation of the British Government, Bismarck argued that the exiled monarch had "in honor" renounced his claim to his dominions. However, but a short time after the vote was granted the king made a public speech in which his royal rights were vigorously asserted. The Government then impounded the indemnity funds, and the problem of what to do with the accruing interest was finally solved by placing it at the Government's disposal as Secret Service funds, with the understanding that it was to be used in frustrating the intrigues of the Guelph faction. Bismarck in one of his pithy expressions declared: "There is nothing of the spy in me, but I think we deserve thanks if we follow evil reptiles into their hiding places to watch what they are doing." Consequently the fund, something like 1,000,000 marks annually, was called the "reptile fund." In course of time the semi-official press received the title of the "reptile press." "But it is not my purpose to go into
the discussion of a question in which
the public is little interested; what
I do care for is the deeply interesting
narrative of a wartime episode in con-
nection with the poem, as told in his
recent correspondence with me. These
are the letters. Read them yourself."


"Thank you, General."


It appears that not long after the
first battle of Bull Run, in which Fon-
taine, the Burt eighteenth Mississippi
Regiment, took part, he was trans-
ferred to the Second Virginia Cavalry,
and at the time of which this narrative
treats was doing picket duty just above
the head of an island near the Seneca
Falls on the Potomac. This was in
August, 1861—one month after Bull
Run.


It was here that Fontaine and another
private named Moore formed close
friendship. Moore was a married man,
and fairly idolized his wife and their
two beautiful young children. Moore
and Fontaine were together, whether
on picket or guard duty. They clung
to each other. They bought little
hand-books of Poems—Byron, Burns,
and others, and together they would
sit in the cool shade of trees or hang-
ing rocks that lined the Potomac above
the Falls of Seneca and read aloud to
each other passages from their favorite
authors.


At this section of the two army lines
the pickets on either side of the waters,
Federal and Confederate, had come to
an understanding and agreement that
there should be no firing at each other
while on picket duty. And but for a
treacherous violation of this contract
by a dastardly soldier, the incident
herewith related would not have oc-
curred, and "All Quiet Along the
Potomac To-night" would never have
been penned. Let me give the story in Fon-
taine's own graphic words:


"I've had to stand on post six hours
at a time. That night I took my stand
at 6, and Moore retired to rest. The
nights were chilly, and we usually kept
some fire burning. There was a small
spring of water close by, and a large
fallen pine tree that I used to sit on
and rest at times, after walking my
beat, and I have frequently stopped at
the spring and bathed my face when
the dreary monotony of the still night
had tendency to lull me to sleep.
As soon as I found that midnight had
arrived I stepped to the fire and threw
on some pine knots, and roused Moore
to take my place.


He rose slowly, picked up his gun,
stepped to the fire and stretched him-
self, as a sleepy soldier will, as I capped
and yawned; and while his arms were
extended, and his hand grasping the
barrel of his gun, there was a flash
across the river and the whiz of a
bullet, and he sank to the earth, with
a hole just above his eye on the left
side, from which flowed a dark, grim
crimson tide. Not a word, not a groan es-
caped him.


I removed his remains from near
the fire where he had fallen. And as
I did so my eyes fell on the telegraphic
column of a newspaper, and it was
headed: 'All Quiet Along the Potomac
Tonight.' And, oh, how truthful it
was! It was certainly all quiet with
me, and with him whom I loved as a
brother.


I could not help shedding a tear,
and my thoughts reverted to his home,
his wife, and his children, and to the
falsehood told by those whose guest I
had been, and whose treachery had
caused his death, and they grew bitter,
and a demon of vengeance arose in me."

STORY OF THE DROWNING ACCIDENT

OFF EAST ROCKAWAY

Steersman White Says There Was an Explosion, and Then a Whirring Sound

How Mr. Caemmerer and His Two Guests Went Down While Swimming.

The naphtha launch Ethel, belonging to Louis J. Caemmerer of East Rockaway, went to the bottom on Sunday afternoon while trying to force passage into Rockaway Bay against a powerful ebb tide. Mr. Caemmerer and his guests, Dr. Read Dennis of Brooklyn and George M. Norwood of Flatbush, were drowned. The party had gone outside for fishing against the advice of friends and fishermen in the bay, who warned them of the dangerous nature of the inlet at ebb tide. Louden White, a young oyster man who accompanied them as steersman, saved himself by swimming seaward and clinging to a buoy, where he was picked up by a yacht. White says there was an explosion in the launch just before the boat went down, which stove a hole in her bottom.

Mr. Caemmerer was in the iron business at 22 DeKalb avenue, Brooklyn, until a few months ago, when he retired. He was about 52 years old, and he had a wife and one child, a six-year-old girl after whom the boat was named. Mr. Dennis was a manufacturer of underwear in Brooklyn and he lived at 465 Clermont avenue with his wife and three children. He was about 35 years old. Mr. Norwood was the manager of the firm of Joseph Norwood & Sons, manufacturers of wire goods at 40 Adams street, Brooklyn. He was unmarried, and he lived with his father, mother, two sisters and three brothers in Flatbush. He had been a member of the Gilbert Dramatic Society of Brooklyn for several years. He was 30 years old.

When Mr. Caemmerer retired from business he built a fine house at East Rockaway and moved there with his family. His brother-in-law, David A. Curtis, a journalist, lived there. He and Mr. Curtis had married sisters. The two were devoted fishermen, and they spent all their Sundays on the bay. Mr. Caemmerer used to own a sailboat, but when he moved to East Rockaway he bought the naphtha launch.

Sailboats were too dependent upon fickle winds to suit him. He purchased the launch from the Gas Engine and Power Company of Morris Dock. It was twenty-five feet long, and had the engine aft. The naphtha was stored forward and had to be pumped into the engine device intended as a guarantee against explosion. The launch cost $525.

Mrs. Caemmerer was much opposed to her husband getting the naphtha launch. She knew that he took big chances on the water. An agent of the manufacturers cruised about him how to handle the launch, and he laughed at his wife's fears.

Sunday Mr. and Mrs. Dennis, with the al separate of his wife and children in New Jersey, had come to Rockaway. As Mr. Caemmerer and his guests were going out, Mr. and Mrs. Dennis were at Hicks Beach. Just within the inlet, to shoot some fish, Mr. Caemmerer, Mr. Norwood, and Dr. Dennis followed in the Ethel, with Louden White at the helm. White knew netting and naphtha as well as anyone. They reached Hicks Beach, and Dennis announced to his guests and their ladies ashore. There were no perils and Dennis said to Caemmerer, "I say, you won't attempt to go outside, will you?" "Oh, guess not," said Mr. Caemmerer. "The inlet is a terrible place on an ebb tide, and I rowed down around the inlet just before you came, and found it pretty rough." After that, White, Caemmerer, Norwood, and Dennis were not seen again.

Both sides of the inlet are shallow and at times boats can enter only by narrow and close passage. At the ebb tide there is tumbling water. At the Waput Point of the inlet, the party moved from spot to spot. Mr. Caemmerer, Mr. Norwood, and Dr. Dennis went out to Long Beach. His guests agreed, and Mr. Caemmerer would not listen to the few warnings. The wind was quiet as they went out, through the inlet and towards the sea. White had a bit of luck and about 4 o'clock came back. There was a mass of swells and breakers; a fresh wind was blowing from the southeast and the Ethel pushed her nose into the east side. She was not to be affected there, and they went around to the Shelter Island side and tried the west.

"It was very rough," said White to a reporter yesterday, "and we were just inside the inlet when there was a whirr, whirr, whirr." There was the whirring sound, and White says to Caemmerer, "Mr. Caemmerer, we can't stand this. Give me an oar, for the water is getting up high." "What, had you shipped water?" asked Caemmerer. "You know it!"

"Where was the hole?"

"Why, in the bottom! That came when the single explosion came. Why, it seemed to be as big as my hand, and the water poured in." "Was it the explosion that blew the hole in the bottom?" L. Sampson.

The institution was opened on September
2nd, and it contains accommodations for
twenty-five boys.

At the time of the presentation of Mr. Samp-
son's report ten boys were inmates of the
school, and since then three or four more boys
have been received.

The average age of the boys is thirteen and
one-half years, the age of the individuals rang-
ing from nine to sixteen years.

The boys receive daily school instructions,
while part of the day is given to manual work
in the tailor shop or about the place.

Sunday religious services are held and the
boys are instructed in the Sunday school les-
sons.

Since the boys have become inmates of the
institution their appearance has greatly
changed and their health has been largely im-
proved.

Major Stiles advocated to remove the insti-
tution as soon as possible to the property
owned by the Association at Laurel Station.

Mr. J. J. Addison has been appointed on
committee of one to communicate with Col-
onel Palmer as to the price for which the Vir-
GINIA Fire and Marine Insurance Company
would be willing to sell five or six acres of
land with a dwelling house adjacent to the
land of the association.

However, no report has as yet been received
on the subject.

According to the statement of Major Stiles
the finances of the organization are in an en-
cumbersome condition, the receipts about bal-
ancing the expenses.

The State pays for the support of the boys
at the rate of twenty-five cents a day, and if
the number of inmates could be brought up to
one hundred, the institution could be made
self-supporting.

In order to do this some changes in the leg-
islation would be necessary, the present laws
being too narrow.

Major Stiles spoke of the inferiority of
institutions of a similar character which he
had visited abroad and expressed himself
especially in favor of the cottage plan, as
introduced in Switzerland and on the Berlin
industrial farm.

To show the advantage of such institutions
Major Stiles called attention to the fact that
two of the inmates, who are not yet fourteen
years old, would have been sent to the pen-
itentiary if it had not been to the existence of
the school.

Hereafter no more boys under fourteen
years of age would be sent to the penitentiary
from this State.

ent officers of the association were reelected
for another year, the vacancy occasioned by
the death of the second vice-president, Mr.
Richard F. Beirne, to be filled by the board
of directors.

The officers of the organization are Robert
Stiles, president; G. Richardson, first vice-
president; W. B. Williams, secretary; John
A. Lancaster, treasurer.

On motion of Mr. Adolphus Blair it was
decided to empower the executive and finance
committees to remove the institution to
Laurel Station, and to negotiate with the
Virginia Fire and Marine Insurance Company
about the purchase of the adjacent property,
if this should be deemed advisable.

Major Stiles stated that the committee of
the Legislature on reduction of criminal ex-
penses had expressed themselves in favor of
the institution and promised to assist it as
much as possible.

DUNBAR AND HIS FRIENDS INFORMAL RECEPTION—A NOTABLE GATHERING AND A SCENE—MS. BERNHARDT AT WORK WITH THE CLAY—HAPPY AND UNAFFECTED.

SCENE FIRST.

Sculptor's studio. Location high and dry. Time 3:15, afternoon of March 20. Light straggles in through two small windows, which in turn afford fine perspectives of a section of cloudy sky, collection of chimneys, network of telegraph wires and other incidental furnishings of modern roof exteriors. The rain keeps up persistent but not unmusical pattering on the roof, slightly monotonous, but it goes well with the sky. General outlook not promising for anything half pleasant. Inside not nearly so bad. All the paraphernalia of the regular workshop of the artist is there. Everybody knows what it is. There are just enough screens to arouse your curiosity as to what is behind them and enough of the recesses to keep you going for hours. On a high shelf there is a collection of plaster casts. A drapery hanging from it makes an effective background for a couch drawn up near the wall, where a lot of big, soft pillows are piled. All the rest of the walls are lined with book racks, paintings, charcoal sketches, plaster casts, squares of tapestry, brocades and a dozen other bits of color. In one corner, on a carpeted platform, is a chair, which has of course a gay piece of drapery across the back. That's the throne, where some people sit to be sculpted. On a mantel are a few old shooting irons, some funny looking pistols, the sort that the banditti carry in the play, and a lot of other interesting, artistic fragments of other days. There hangs a Japanese umbrella; here haunts a gay ribbon; in short, just the very kind of interior which looks well in a picture and nowhere else, except by the freight. The central point of attraction is the easel in the middle of the floor. Resting on the shelf is a square board, covered two inches thick with red clay. Rough outlines of a woman's head are formed on it. A century-old chair is drawn up near the easel as if the artist had but just arisen. Within reach is the big tin of wet clay and all the utensils which help the fingers to fashion shapes and forms.

SCENE SECOND.

The portiere at the door parts and the actors in our little drama enter. The sculptor with hospitable smiles of welcome makes his guests very much at home. Upon one of them, a sister artist, all attention centers. She moves forward to the rough image in clay on the easel, sees with satisfaction the cleverness it displays, takes the artist's chair and begins herself to mold the yielding clay to suit her own fancy. With every touch of her deft fingers she makes it more like her own profile and most perfect likeness; the mood for work had passed and she stopped. Still she sits there, with the light seeming to radiate rather in her wavy, yellow hair. Her attire is black—the soberest of black. She speaks rapidly of many things; compliments the sculptor; points out the fine lines in the bust nearby; fondles the little girls who come near her; poses, yes, just a bit, perhaps, but then she is Sarah Bernhardt.

HOW IT ALL CAME ABOUT.

This little comedy was played on the boards of Mr. Dunbar's studio yesterday afternoon before a small but intensely appreciative audience, which included Messrs. Johnston, Weyl and Brooke, and it was one of the finest scenes in which Bernhardt has appeared the past week. The more so because it was almost unexpected, that is, for yesterday's bill. The proposition, slightly venerable, that children of genius recognize each other seems to have ill bearing on this case. Mr. Dunbar, in an interview with the actress early in the week, received from her a promise to visit his studio. Thursday afternoon at 2:30 was the hour set. The news got around the top floor of the building in which is located the studio, and all the busy women workers on the floor found it convenient to pass by the door that Bernhardt was to enter just as often as they could. But the gifted Bernhardt spent all day Thursday in bed, though few suspected that fact in her splendid representation of Fedora that evening. Yesterday she kept her promise. Mr. Dunbar called at the Arlington for her, and merry company they made driving down to the studio, Mrs. Grau, her little girl Nile, Seylor and little Regina helping to fill the carriage to overflowing. When they reached their destination and finally the grand entree of the party into the studio of the sculptor, Mr. Dunbar did not have as much to say as he might owing to the slight knowledge he has of French and the equally frail support that the English gives to his talented visitor. But they got on pretty well, nevertheless.

"Monsieur Dunbar, work here?" said Bernhardt, taking in all the room in one swift glance. "Petite?" and the interrogation in her bright eyes needed no interpretation.

Two artist friends then helped to carry the burden of conversation with the rest of the company. Mr. Dunbar led his visitor up to the easel, where the foundation of what he expected to make her portrait gave her great surprise and pleasure. The face was formed and the hair laid on in rough knots. It needed the expression and the likeness. For these the sculptor wanted the sitting. Instead of that Bernhardt herself began to model the soft clay. With dexterous touches she changed the shape of the head and arranged the wavy locks in another style—all this with her gloves on. Discovering that in each turn she gave the clay there was, indeed, the impression of the seam in the finger of her glove, she pulled it off and with greater freedom worked life in her clay and the likeness was unmistakable. It is a rough cast but it is Bernhardt. She stopped just short of the finishing touches. Mr. Dunbar will keep it just as it is, a treasured specimen of artistic skill and a browning touch to his collection in the studio. Next fall when she comes here again she has promised him a sitting.

Bernhardt's manner charming. She enjoyed the visit and the chance to work again in a studio. When she rests in Paris, painting and modelling are her chief relaxation. Yesterday it made an agreeable diversion on her way to a Cleopatra rehearsal. She fingered as long as she dared and then, with regrets on both sides, concluded her visit with many expressions of admiration for Mr. Dunbar's talent and the pleasure it would give her to come again. After she had gone everybody remembered some fine phrase or word they might have said with great satisfaction to all concerned, but the words of one, "It was completely floored," explained the situation perfectly. It was Bernhardt matinee. The great artist was seen at her best—simple, unaffected, true to her role, happy in the pleasure it gave others, satisfied in the opportunity it gave herself. Her audience suffered no distractions, for Bernhardt filled the horizon. Each had something to say to her to the measure of their ability to discuss art in French, but the star held the boards and the rest were content to listen.

proved of it, including the insurance
feature.

Kansas City will be the distributing
point, and all goods will be purchased
direct from the manufacturers. In
every county where the Alliance will
pledge its support a store manager
will be appointed and goods supplied
by the National Union company for
share in the profits. The National
Union company is an outgrowth of the
Ocala convention. The scheme was
sprung then and approved by President
Polk. Three months later a meeting of
capitalists was held in New York city
and the company was formed and
$5,000,000 of the capital stock was sub-
scribed. It is probable that the work of
appointing agents will begin Immedi-
ately, and the first stores will be estab-
lished the 1st of next January.

Everything was fixed in caucus before
the convention proceeded to the election
of officers. The various candidates and
leaders met at noon to arrange a slate.
President McGrath stated that he de-
sired an endorsement of his official acts
and acquittal of the various charges of
corruption which had been made against
him. He did not wish to be the cause
of discord in the party, and he would
withdraw in favor of W. H. Ut-
ley, state treasurer. The other
candidates agreed to this compromise.

The programme miscarried, however,
as far as the election of the president
was concerned. Some members who had
not been admitted to the caucus pro-
posed that no nominating speeches be
made, and that an informal ballot be
taken. The motion prevailed, and it
was found that Utley, W. H. Biddle and
Z. H. Maxon led, while seven others re-
quired to address the convention,
and to swear to support the Cincinnati
platform, the sub-treasury and the co-
operative schemes.

several ballots the contest narrowed
down to Biddle, Utley and Maxon. Then
McGrath gave the word for Maxon to
withdraw in Utley's favor, but all of
Maxon's friends did not or would not
understand the order, and enough of
them cast their votes for Biddle to elect
him and to defeat Utley. The result
was a great surprise, particularly to
McGrath, who could not see in it any
endorsement or vindication.

Dr. McLain, of Topeka, however,
smoothed things over by proposing a
resolution expressing unqualified con-
fidence in the retiring president. The
resolution was unanimously adopted.
President Biddle is forty-five years of
age, was a soldier in the Union army,
and is now stock raiser from Butler
county. He is practically unknown in
the politics of the state. Mrs. Fannie
X. Vickery was chosen to succeed her-
self as vice president, and J. S. French
was elected secretary.

The Old Resort Comes in for a Good


Share of Visitors.


There was the usual complement of
visitors at Long Beach, yesterday, that
is to say, the beach was crowded,
women and children predominating.
There was also fair sprinkling OF male
adults of tn e sober minded variety. The
surf was very mild, and the bath houses
were taxed to their utmost capacity. So
great was the demand for bath rooms,
that as high as eight persons,
in some cases, were compelled
to use the same room at one
time. This was somewhat un-
pleasant, but the crowd was good hu-
mored and there was no grumbling.
The last two Sund ays have demonstrate
ed that Long Beach lacks bath house
capacity, although when the season
opened it was thought ample facilities
had been provided. The fact is Long
Beach Is regaining her old-time popular
ity as bathing resort, and the crowds
that frequent the place are constantly
increasing. To accommodate the null
titudes comfortably more bath houses
should be provided.


The water perhaps, never was in bet
ter condition than yesterday, and every
body had good time. The juvenile
bathers were legion, and to say that the
children enjoyed themselves is putting
it mildly. Long Beach always will have
the reputation of being the best and
safest of all the beaches for children.
The orderliness and respectability of the
crowds that congregate there, are also in
it's favor, and make it the ideal family
resort.

LONDON, Oct. 12.--The National League in Great Britain has issued the following manifesto:

Some months ago the members of this executive body were appointed by Charles Stewart Parnell to advance the cause of Irish independence. Great Britain fighting under great uncertainties, we held our ground and rallied every Irishman who remained true to the principle for which our leader lived and died—the principle of an Independent Irish party and an independent Irish parliament. Ireland has received a blow by the death of Mr. Parnell from which it cannot recover for a generation. When Daniel O'Connell died all was chaos; a parliamentary party sprung up, but failure and disgrace marked its course. Nothing was done for Ireland and the name of an Irish member in parliament became a byword. Fenianism arose and so was changed Irish affairs; absorbed the attention of parliament, while Irishmen died for Ireland on the scaffold or perished in prison or exile. Something was then done.

The English state church in Ireland disappeared and the next step was taken in the tardy course of legislation for the protection of the Irish tenant. The power of Fenianism was for the moment broken, but not until it had revived the spirit of Irish nationality.

Parliamentary agitation followed the momentary subsistence of the Fenian movement and once more failure marked its course.

Then Charles Stewart Parnell came, and all was changed. Rallying the force of Irish nationality and everywhere combining revolutionary action with constitutional agitation, he fixed the attention of the civilized world upon the wrongs and miseries of Ireland. English parties and English leaders bowed before him.

The Tories vied with the Liberals to gain his support. Firm and inexorable, commanding followers whom he found rabble and of whom he made an army, he dictated his terms to the English prime minister and the ministers. In ten years he did more for Ireland than had been done in generations. Measure after measure, bearing his mark, took its place on the statute books, and his work was crowned when the prime minister of England brought into parliament a bill to establish an Irish parliament.

He is gone. Ireland mourns over his grave today. What is the duty of those he left behind? What is the duty of the men who followed him to the last in his struggle for Irish freedom?

It has been said that we fought for a man, not for principle. It is not true. We fought for the principle which the man embodied. The man himself was indeed, a principle—the principle of self-reliance and independence which nothing could sap. To that principle we are stanch. It is now necessary for the members of this organization to elect a new president and new executive committee, and we invite the branches of the National League in Great Britain to take immediate steps to this end. We urge our fellow countrymen not to despair if victory seems distant. We ask them to take their motto, the last words addressed by Mr. Parnell to the executive committee: Hold on tight.

on Friday, for an injury to her
hand caused by an explosion of fire-
works, was given carbolic acid in mis-
take for whisky. She died in a few
minutes.


Citizens of St. Paul have secured sub-
scriptions to the amount of $250,000
toward the fund for the Democratic
national convention, in case it is held in
that city. Of this amount 100,000 is
for the remodelling and enlarging of
the auditorium.


William H. Goodrich, for 25 years
business manager of the Hartford
Journal, has sold his entire interest in
the paper and its building to his associ-
ates, Senator Hawley, Charles Dudley
Warner and Charles Hopkins Clark, and
has retired from the concern.


The Santa Fe vestibuled limited train
which left Chicago at 8 o'clock Satur-
day evening, was derailed at Bear Creek
Mo., early Sunday morning, and five
cars went down steep embankment.
No one was killed, but a number of per-
sons were seriously injured.


Arrangements have been made by the
Wabash Railroad Company to enter
Pittsburg over the tracks of the Pitts-
burg & Western road. The connection
will be made at Defiance, O., and line
service will be pulled to Pittsburg &
Western at that point.


Robert Moore, aged 30 years, son of a
wealthy contractor of Cincinnati, went
into a hardware store in that city on
Saturday morning, bought a revolver
and had it loaded. He then said: "I
want to see how it works," and placing
it to his temple fired. He died almost
instantly.


An Erie railway transfer float, loaded
with 10 cars carrying 100 head of cattle
while being towed up the East river, at
New York Sunday, struck on Black
Rock. A hole was stove in the float,
causing it to sink, and 45 head of cattle
were drowned. The loss is estimated at
$4,000.


The Colored Voters League of Alle-
gheny county, Pa., has issued a mani-
festo calling upon their brethren to take
some action to overthrow the poll
ticians who have steadily used the col-
ored citizens of this country as mere
political tools to forward their self-
serving schemes.


A dispatch from Meridian, Miss., says
that on Thursday night William Wright
and a Miss Phillips were married, and
that while the attendant festivities were
in progress a man named Johnson,
rival of Sutton, came to the window and
shot and killed Wright. The murderer
escaped.


One of the engines on the Sixth
avenue elevated railway jumped the
track at Park Place, Sunday, and the
train crashed into the rear of one of the
blocked trains. The rear car of the
latter was derailed, and but for the
guard rails would have fallen over into
the street. No one was injured.


W. H. Pearsall, wife and family lying
near Goldsboro, N. C., were burned
to death in their dwelling on Tuesday
last. The bodies were discovered on
Saturday. Weightman Thompson, a
former rejected suitor of the murdered
man's wife, has been arrested on sus-
picion of having committed the crime.


The mangled body of Judge George
W. McLain, of the circuit court of St.
Joseph, Missouri, was found on Satur-
day in an open court in the centre of
the court house. It is supposed he fell
from a walk 60 feet above, on Thurs-
day, while on his way to his cour-
room. He had been missing since that
day.


A dispatch from Pittsburg says that
negotiations are in progress for the pur-
chase of the Hostetter Coke Company's
plant by the Frick Coke Company. The
price to be paid is said to be $800,000
in bonds of the latter concern. If the
deal is closed it will give the Frick Com-
pany almost monopoly of the Con-
necuticut Coke trade.


The main building of the Eastern
Michigan Insane Asylum, at Pontiac,
was burned on Saturday. No lives were
lost, so far as known, but scores of the
poor lunatics, who were forced to stand
in the bitterly cold blizzard for hours
before they could be housed, have suf-
fered severely. Many, it is believed, es-
caped to the woods during the excite-
ment. Searching parties have gone in
quest of them. The loss is placed at
$100,000.


It was stated in New Haven on Sat-
urday that "the supreme court is di-
vided in the Morris vs. Bulkley quo-
warranto suit; that Judges Seymour,
Fen and Carpenter are of the opinion
that the law and equity of the case is
in favor of Judge Morris, while Chief
Justice Andrews and Judge Torrence
are of the opinion that the court has no
jurisdiction." Judge Seymour is said
to be writing the majority opinion and
Chief Justice Andrews the minority.

A rough brick chimney, rather rudely constructed, standing on the brick yard grounds, at the foot of Sixteenth street attracted the attention of Herald representatives yesterday afternoon, while strolling about the outskirts of the city. Seated near the brick chimney was an individual who was engaged in placing wood in the furnace. In reply to inquiries, the fireman said that the chimney or oven had been constructed for the purpose of experimenting with the clay in this part of the country, with the ultimate view of establishing a pottery and tile works in this neighborhood. While the reporter was engaged in conversation a third individual joined the party, and the fireman turned to the new comer and stated that he was the gentleman under whose directions the experiments were being made.

The reporter immediately recognized the gentleman as Mr. Hankins, who attracted so much attention at the Portland Industrial exposition last year by taking what seemed to be pieces of mud and shaping and forming flower pots, jugs, plates and thousand other articles. Crowds surrounded his booth at all times, and Mr. Hankins' skill excited wonder and attention.

Mr. Hankins led the reporter to a frame building standing on the edge of the brick yard. Within the building on a wooden table were a number of pots, jugs and other articles. In one corner of the room a lathe used by potters had been placed, while clay, graphite, silica and other material was stored in profusion.

In conversation with the reporter Mr. Hankins spoke of the wonderful resources of this section of the country that he was determined to experiment with the clay providing any could be found, and if his experiments proved successful he intended to establish a pottery in this vicinity. He was satisfied that the blue clay found in the bay in inexhaustible quantity would prove valuable for such common articles as flower pots and tiling, but he intended to make an effort to find material for making sewer pipe, fire bricks, fine earthenware, etc. To this end he secured clay from the vicinity of Lake Samish and also the Fairhaven coal mine.

As the result of his first experiment, Mr. Hankins exhibited brick which he said would stand about 500 degrees of heat. The brick was perfectly formed, and the only difference between it and the English fire brick was that the latter is of a lighter color. The difference in color was explained by the fact that the percentage of silica was greater in the English brick. The high standard attained by the English brick is the result of several hundred years labor, but for the first experiment, Mr. Hankins thinks the brick manufactured by him is superior to any he has seen in this country.

The greatest interest is attached to the experiments being made with sewer pipe. If the proper quality of pipe can be made here it will result in the saving of thousands of dollars to the city when the proposed sewage system will be constructed. Mr. Hankins is firmly convinced that he will be able to make as good, strong and endurable pipe as is made anywhere on the coast.

Silica is one of the most important ingredients needed and an eight foot vein of it was encountered in the Fairhaven coal mine. Graphite figures largely in the manufacture of earthenware and this is found in unlimited quantities on the line of the Fairhaven and Southern. The experiments made have been very satisfactory and, without doubt, is expressed of its ultimate success. Mr. Hankins is a practically experienced and skillful potter and his experiments are conducted in a thorough manner.

Special TO the Gazette.


GALVESTON, TEX, June 4.—About 1
O'Clock this afternoon a colored woman was
grabbing on the brick wharf. A gust of
wind blew her hat off. Charles Schadd,
sometimes called Johnson, fisherman and
crabber by occupation, attempted to catch
it for her, but it went over into the bay.
He picked up a cane and, while standing
on the edge of the wharf attempting to
fish the hat out, James Brown, better
known as Fisherman Brown, stepped
up behind him and pushed him
overboard into the bay, saying
"Now, you—off for a swim for it."
Schadd rose but once. He was a colored
man of middle age and is said to have been
of an inoffensive disposition. Brown was
shortly after arrested and lodged in jail
on a charge of murder. He is a native of
the island of St. Helena, and takes a very
complacent view of the matter, and con-
tends that Schadd deserved mis-
fate. Ill
feeling has existed between the two men
for some time, and Brown threatened to
throw Schadd overboard some day, which
he did to-day with fatal effect. Schadd's
body is still undiscovered.

was a high arch of evergreens, trimmed about
with red and blue bunting. Just
under the arch were the words in Roman char
acters "Gut Heil". The gallery all around the
room was entirely hidden behind the deep green
decorations, and at regular distances along the
wall were large pictures of the famous German
composers, Wagner, Mendelssohn and Beethoven
and other noted men who have brought honor
upon the German nation by their great works.


This is the fourth turnfest of the North Pacific
Turn Bezirk. The first session was opened at
o'clock yesterday afternoon with President
William Wagner presiding. The following del
egates were present:


Portland—L. Dammasch, T. L. Rung, R. Krohn,
J. Luger, C. Hoeber.


Tacoma—H. L. Fuhrberg, T. Stance, N. J. Sic
bert.


Spokane—C. Juckeland, A. Potter, Rob Keller.


Centralia—M. Hochstatter, A. Fuss.


Seattle—A. Miller, D. Rohlfs, C. Hubert, Fl.
Schroeder, L. Meyer, Fl. T. Heuss.


The first and most important business of the
meeting was the election of new officers. The
result was as follows: President, D. Rohlfs, of
Seattle; vice president, Fl. O. Fuhrberg, of Ia
coma; secretary, H. Schroeder, of Seattle; as
sistant secretary, C. Juckeland, of Spokane.


According to the reports of the officers, the
turn society is in a very prosperous condition,
numerically and financially. Considerable dis
cussion was had over minor amendments to the
regulations and rules of the society. The sub
ject of practical gymnastics and mental and
moral training was also dwelt upon at length.


The next turnfest will be held at Portland,
and that city made the administrative head
quarters of the North Pacific Turn Verein.
After hearty vote of thanks to the retiring
officers for their faithful services the meeting
adjourned.


In the evening the members and delegates
held a commerce or convivial gathering. Fol-
lowing is the programme for today and for Mon
day and Tuesday:


Sunday a. m., Turner hall—Concert by Pro-
fessor Luebens orchestra, prize contest, consist
ing of singing (male chorus), fencing, Indian
club swinging, recitations; gymnastic exhibit
ion by members of the visiting Turners and
Seattle Turn Verein.


Monday at Leschi park—9 s. h., at the pa
vilion, prize turning on the various apparatus:
Horizontal and parallel bars, vaulting-horse and
iron wand exercises; 3 p. m. prize aquatic
sports on Lake Washington, consisting of swim
ming, boat racing, and fishermen's tournament,
(entirely new in Seattle); refreshments and
lunch at the Casino furnished by the Seattle
Turnverein. Admission free to everybody.


Monday evening at Turner hall—Grand ball
and distribution of prizes.


Tuesday afternoon—2 p. m., excursion by
steamer Kirk and around Lake Washington
(Take Yesler avenue cars to Lake Washington).

MONUMENT TO JEFFERSON DAVIS

ATLANTA, Ga. May 15.—Gen. Gordon has issued the following general order to his confederate brethren,

CONFEDERATE VETERANS,

ATLANTA, GA. May 10, 1891.

MY CONFEDERATE BROTHERS—Upon you now rests in large measure the responsibility for raising funds for the proposed monument to the memory of Jefferson Davis.

NO argument, no urgent appeal, no special effort on our part is needed to secure your hearty cooperation in this cause. You will esteem it not only sacred duty but high privilege to enlist in this work and to secure the aid of all of our people throughout the Union. With unfaltering fidelity to every interest of our whole country and sincere appreciation of all great Americans of every section, we will build monuments to our own peerless heroes as an inspiration to the coming generations, and we will erect a fitting one to our great chieftain, whose public and private life was without fear or reproach; whose services to his country in peace and in war will yet command the respect and win the plaudits of all his countrymen, and whose dauntless devotion to his convictions has scarcely a parallel in history.

The details of the plans for raising the necessary money may safely be entrusted to the different local organizations, but the committee appointed by the Southern Press Association, itself largely composed of Confederate veterans, has issued a call for the people to take steps to forward the cause of voluntary contributions or other methods which they may deem best. This seems to me both opportune and wise. I therefore most respectfully and earnestly urge all Confederate organizations to meet on that day for this purpose, and all Confederates not members of any organization to unite with the people and assist the movement in their respective localities.

The funds raised by special efforts of Confederates may be sent to Judge W. L. Calhoun, Atlanta, Ga., who will act as treasurer, issue receipts for all remittances, and place the same in a bank to the credit of the Davis monument fund.

J. B. GORDON,

Commanding U. S. Confederate Veterans.

The cooperation of the sons of Confederate veterans, and especially patriotic Southern women, is invited and assured.

J. B. GORDON.

To the Editor of the Eagle


Sarah Jane Stimson Reeves was born
May 10, 1827, near Halifax Court House,
Virginia, and died Feb. 6, 1891, in her
last year of consumption. She bore her
affection without a murmur for five years
and was confined to her bed for five
months prior to her death. She was mar-
ried Aug. 25, 1854, to John H. Reeves in
Muscoe county, Ind., but was left a
widow at his death April 9, 1874. She en-
dured the hardships of widowed life
courageously and was never heard to com-
plain of the burdens she had to assume
in caring for the family. Her sole object
was to lead a pure Christian life and by
her example, bring up her two sons, the
only children, to respected and useful
manhood. Her younger son was taken
away in his youth, with the same disease
on Aug. 8, 1890; the other, A. W. Reeves,
who is well and favorably known in this
city, remains to mourn her loss. She
united with the Methodist Episcopal
church when quite a young girl and was a
devoted Christian until the end.


The life of woman in many instances is
not as eventful as the life of man, but
when we look upon the life work of true
womanly woman, an exemplary wife and
mother, well can we say the world is in-
finitely better by her having lived.

Thursday of every month. The change from
the Court House, where meetings, and con-
sequently small meetings could only be held
during the day, is hailed by the members
with much pleasure. The society has not
had the encouragement its educative force
should receive. Now pleasant rooms and
the evenings, when the busiest man can find
some leisure, are expected to be the salvation
and growth of the society. The first
meeting in Carnegie Hall will be to-night at
7:30.


The most notable wedding of the season
took place at the First Baptist Church, McKeesport
last night. Miss Viola Haney,
daughter of Mrs. Lewis Haney, of that place
was married to Mr. John L. Getty, promi-
nent attorney of Indiana, Pa. There were
large number of friends from all over the
State in attendance. The bride was attended
by four bridesmaids in charming costume.
After the ceremony a reception and supper
was held at the residence of W. W. Hunter.
The young couple went East on an extended
tour, and on their return will make their
home at Indiana.


Social Chatter.


Mr. GEORGE S. GRAHAM, popular young
Pittsburg business man, left on the Eastern
express on Tuesday morning, accompanied
by party of Friends bound for Boston. On
Thursday noon Mr. Graham is to wed.

Is it possible that the people of that section, and business men too, are made to suffer for the gratification of one or two men, or for the sake of few dollars? It seems so from all appearances. THE Emperor Of Germany has criticised
his uncle. the Prince of Wales, with such
severity concerning the baccarat scandal.
that, says the telegraphic dispatches, it is
likely to create bad blood between the
two, and break off the contemplated
visit of the Emperor to his grandmother.
Queen Victoria. But this can hardly be.
Victoria is not likely to offend the Kaiser
because of the disgruntled Prince. If she
should intimate to her grandson that his
visit would be unwelcome, it would
amount to breach of international good
manners that might result seriously to
both nations. Possibly the garden party
contemplated in honor of the Kaiser by
the Prince of Wales may be abandoned.
That much the Queen could not prevent,
and for that bit of i'll will the Emperor
need not particularly care. But it is
rather with the gossips than with the re-
liable news that there is any thought that
the Prince of Wales is so angered as to
affront his nephew for the cause stated.
Moreover, it is developing that Wales has
not been nearly SO much concerned over
the baccarat scandal as the news has
made out, and the latest advices also are
that wave of reaction has already set in
IN his favor. As rule the early specula-
tons of the sensational reporters concern
ing social affairs in Europe are to be
taken with broad margin of allowance
for imaginings. Indeed, it is quite the
safest plan TO await the second and cooler
advices in all these cases.

ant recollections these characters bring

est heaven of happiness would have

read every Christmas that plum pud-

How the Smithsonian People Were Fooled
by a Graphophone's Letter.

DR. R. L. GARNER of Roanoke, Va., is con-
vinced of the fact that monkeys have artic-
ulate speech like that of human beings and
differing from the latter only in development.
He has been experimenting of late with the
graphophone in this connection, securing a
"record" of squeaks and chattering by one
monkey and subsequently grinding them out
through a trumpet for the benefit of another
monkey, in order to observe what remarks were
elicited from the second monkey in response.
In this way he has hoped to gradually make up
a lexicon of the monkey language, which would
probably not be very voluminous, inasmuch as
the simian vocabulary does not appear to con-
tain more than about forty words. The doctor
thinks that he has already secured five of them.

The other day DR. Garner suffered a severe
pang in consequence of misunderstanding in-
cidental to a correspondence which he has been
conducting with the Smithsonian Institution
apropos of this monkey business. He sent a
letter to DR. Baker of the Smithsonian in the
usual business form in the shape of a grapho-
phone cylinder, beginning: Roanoke, Va.
My dear sir, &c. DR. Baker put the cylinder
upon his own graphophone, knowing by the
superscription on the envelope that it was from
DR. Garner, and turned on the electromotor
attached with much interest, anticipating some
communication of importance regarding mon-
key talk.

Unfortunately he put on the cylinder wrong
end foremost, the result being that DR. Garner's
letter came out backward. DR. Baker up to
this time had been sceptic regarding the
theory of the gentleman from Roanoke, but
upon hearing this rendering of the communications
in question he supposed it was a monkey
record and became at once convinced that
there was more in the idea than he had origin-
ally supposed. He even went so far as to say
that there was an unmistakable semblance of
articulate speech in the record, although he
was unable to understand the remarks.

DR. Garner was in town three days ago and
enlightened DR. Baker on the subject, after the
latter, expert in zoology, and his assistants had
ground of the supposed monkey talk in the
manner described some scores of times. He
explained that there was something in the idea
after all, as unintentionally adopted by his
friend, inasmuch as in the case there was an il-
lustration to be found of evolution backward
from the language of man to the speech of the
monkeys.

MONKEY AND CHILD.

DR. Garner said to STAR reporter the other
day that in his opinion monkey talk was quite
a highly developed speech, considering the fact
that the monkey has no such facilities for the
development of language as are enjoyed by
human beings. As he expressed it, the speech
of monkeys is almost wholly vowel; so, for
that matter, is the human infant. But it must
be remembered that the child has the superior
advantage of education for its vocal organs
from the cradle, not to mention an hereditary
experience of the use of those organs through
ever so many generations. When you hear an
ignorant person speak of instinct in animals
you ought to know that he means hereditary
and transmitted experience or practice. It
seems wonderful, under the circumstances,
that the more intelligent monkeys should have
so many as forty words, approximately speak-
ing, at their command.

In trying to find out what a monkey says
according to DR. Garner, there is difficulty, to
begin with, from the very fact that the conso-
nant elements of its language are absent. What
it has to say is expressed by squeaks and other
sounds not to be comprehended off-hand. In
one case, there is a monkey word for food; but
it is not to be expressed in type otherwise
than by phrasing it in this wise: "E-e-f-f
sharpe." That gives a notion of the word to
any person who knows music; it can hardly be
conveyed otherwise.

THE MONKEY'S RESPONSE.

Make that sound to a monkey and it will al-
ways respond in some fashion, because it knows
that food of some sort is meant. The other
four words which DR. Garner has thus far se-
cured for his monkey lexicon are "pain,"
"satisfaction," "fear" and "menace." It is simply
a question, he thinks, of going on from this
point and discovering the other words of the
limited vocabulary of our arboreal cousins.

It seems, as he states the fact, that in the
monosyllabic vocabulary of monkeys there are
no negatives. Furthermore, emphasis is made
in no other fashion than by the repetition of
one utterance. Also, a single utterance slightly
varied means many things, accentuation trans-
forming nouns into verbs, and so on. One obj-
ect of the investigation of this subject is to
discover whether monkey talk represents the
incipiency of human language as it exists today
or not. One thing DR. Garner thinks very cer-
tainly, that the language of monkeys at
present is well developed as is the animal
itself, compared with civilized man.

Once the lexicon of monkey words is obtained, Dr.
Garner believes that it will be practicable to
establish intelligent communication with mon-
keys, and as to the possibilities to be secured
in this way of humanizing the anthropoid apes,
in particular, only the widest speculations can
be induced.

The Oregon Express was also held unhappily by the landslides north of Coos Bay. The Soldier Special, bringing in the First United States Infantry back to San Francisco, will arrive here to-day.

The returns are not all in, but when the accounts are made up and figures cast together for the careful perusal of Executive Boards, the damage statements will in all probability show Southern California as the heaviest losers by the great storm. Between Barstow and San Diego, and Los Angeles, the damage has been particularly extensive; and a large force of men is working on repairs. Mr. Bissell thinks that trains can be run between Los Angeles and San Diego by to-morrow noon.

The Empress of India has arrived at Ceylon, and her passengers will spend a week inhaling the tropic breezes of the Indian isle. Leaving this point, the steamship will cross the Bay of Bengal to Penang and thence through the Straits of Malacca to Singapore, which is the center of the Malay. General Manager Robinson of the Atlantic and Pacific arrived from the South last evening and is at the Palace.

Montana is about the only state in the Union which has placed the Australian ballot reform law upon its statute, with all its ironclad features. All states have the law more or less, but all preserve its essential principle, the secrecy of the ballot. There is a deal of red tape to unwind and a deal of circumlocution to observe in carrying out the strict letter of the law. It imposes many needless formalities and ceremonies upon voters and officers of elections, and works hardships upon electors in sparsely populated portions of the state, but it preserves the secret ballot and on this account its objectionable features have been accepted with but little murmuring. Many improvements may be made in it, without lowering the barrier; it secures the voter from the watchful eye of the shift boss or professional voter. They will doubtless be made in time, but the perfect election law for this corrupt day and generation may look for it when the "purification of politics" is not regarded by some great party leaders as an idle dream.

While, as has been stated, many in the Union have placed the Australian election law upon their statute books, and while no two of them are exactly similar in their provisions, yet all guarantee the secrecy of the ballot. It has been left for the republican legislature of the great state of Pennsylvania to enact what it is pleased to term the Australian ballot reform system, but it really reforms nothing, leaving, as it does, the voter to the mercy of the boss and briber. It is a vicious law which should not receive the approval of the governor of that state. The democrats in the Legislature attempted to ensure the secrecy which is the important feature of the Australian law but were defeated by Boss Quay and his republican strikers in the Legislature. The Law which was passed allows the voter to take another voter with him into the booth; he is not to be sworn or even questioned as to what constitutes his incapacity to mark his ballots. He simply offers the plea that he cannot properly mark them. That is enough to admit the briber or employer into the booth with the willing victim and in the secrecy permitted the ticket can be made suitable to all hands.

It will be admitted that this is a departure upon the Australian voting system. It defeats the very object of the law. The employer who wishes to control the votes of his men has in this method the way opened to him. A mercenary or dependent voter can be led or coerced into accepting the briber or boss as his companion in the booth. Under the provisions of said law the great iron kings and coal barons of Pennsylvania can control the votes of the dependent or bribe-taker quite easily and with greater success than they could under the old system of "party tickets." And yet our republican brethren claim they are the true friends of the Australian reform ballot law.

Farmers stables are rarely con-
structed with view to healthfulness;
are usually deficient in light. ventila-
ton and drainage. These defects give
rise to much evil to animals confined
In them and disorders of some kind
are likely to result. Want of light or
light in struggling rays from various
small inlets Injuries the eyesight and
where there is insufficient light, there
is almost surely insufficient ventila-
ton. Stables thus closely built do
not admit of free circulation of air.
consequently they become filed with
foul air. impregnated with~the pun
gent vapors arising from manure,
which constantly breathed, irritates
the mucous membranes of the throat
and lungs, and keeps them in a more
or less infamed condition And if
drainage is insufficient, and absorbents
are not supplied. the floor becomes
filed with urine-s saturated manure
which increases these disagreeable
vapors.


Stables should be built on some
what elevated ground; if low and fat
the site should be well-drained; this
would be well if done in any case.
Where no other than an earth floor is
had, absorbents should be used in
abundance, especially if the stable be
q low, close one. But it is better to
have good floors. Wood floors of
thick, solid material, do well enough.
The floor should have slight inclina-
ton from front to rear, the seams
between the planks covered with other
plank, to prevent the liquids getting
beneath the floor. Underneath the
terminus of the floor at the rear should
be placed gutter to receive and car
ry off the liquids to the manure pile.
If good and lasting floor be desired,
concrete is the most economical in
the long run. These, too, should have
few inches inclination to the rear
with drains to serve the purpose of
carrying off the liquids. The follow
ing method makes a good concrete
floor:


Take out the earth to about foot
in depth, fill in with course gravel;
smooth this off to proper grade, say
four inches in ten feet. Upon this
put small stones-cobble stones-and
press down solid. making drains where
required. Over this, when raised up
sufficiently high and firm, spread a
layer of mortar, press In the top of
this, when half dry, some sand and
to add to the thickness and durability
of the floor, more mortar and sand
may be put on; instead of mortar,
some use gas tar, then finish off with
sand. Stables are often built too low,
overhead is put down too low. This
floor should be at least eight feet
high; it gives better ventilation, and
instead of letting the light and air
struggle in as best it may through
small apertures there should be made
one or two long windows reaching
we'll up to the ceiling or upper floor
The sash in them should be swung on
pivots in the middle, so that the sash
may be swung out at top; this gives
better ventilation, the vapor within
escaping at top and the fresh air ad-
mitted at bottom. The windows
should be in front, as side lights are
hurtful to the eyes of stock, especially
if there be no light on the opposite
side. It costs but little more either of
money or labor to erect such comfort
able stables. and certainly nothing is
lost by it. The proper saving of the
manure in this way the ammonia that
otherwise would be lost repays much
besides the advantage and profit aris-
ing from having good, sound, healthy
stock. Ohio Farmer.

New HAVEN, Feb. 8.

Bushnell of this city, Vice-President of the Ericsson Coast Defense Company, which has the old Destroyer taken out of Brooklyn for repairs says: We are fitting up the vessel for the purpose of testing a gun that will fire underwater. dealers are first rendered unrecogniz-
able. If the animal has long hair, he
is clipped; if he is black and white, the
stealer blackens him all over with a dye
mixture that holds its color for several
weeks. Short haired dogs have their
ears and tails cut. The dealers who
sell these dogs may be frequently seen
in the Champs Elysees, the Bots de
Boulogne or in the public gardens, lead
ing five or six animals at a time. Other
dealers make their trades at the dog
markets, of which there are two-on
Sunday afternoons at the horse market
on the Boulevard Port Royal, and on
Tuesdays at the bird market on the
Quai aux Fleurs. The dealers pay a
tax of three cents for each place occu-
pied by a dog.-Paris Cor. New York
Epoch

We have been shown a curious shoe,
owned by N. Bunker, of Newbury.

demolished, which was built in

heel are one piece, and made of

somewhat ornamental. It is one of

Trenton. JAN. 10. 1891.—The matter of much misrepresented and misunderstood is that the State Board of Agriculture has decided to give considerable attention to the subject at the annual meeting the end of this month. Dir. H. N. J. Hunt of the State Board of Health, has been invited to deliver an address on the subject and it is known that he will to some extent criticise the present laws controlling pleuro-pneumonia. Information is at hand that the United States Government has spent $800,825 to hold the disease in check in New Jersey alone. The authorities here are disposed to think that there has been considerable waste in the expenditure of money.

The State Board of Health still continues to have control of the quarantine of diseased cattle, but has no power to condemn or slaughter herds. Little or no tuberculosis has come to the knowledge of the department during the year, not over fifty-five cases. The whole county of Hudson is in quarantine because it is a notable trading point for cattle, and the avenue through which all the trouble has come. It is there that nearly all the money is spent and the doctrine of condemnation and appraisement very largely pursued. It is alleged that more cattle are killed than is necessary.

The United States reports that 50 cattle were slaughtered and paid for at cost of $12,896.25. This expenditure is regarded as superfluous, as it is not necessary to kill so many cattle in an affected herd. The disease is only contagious where the cows are brought in direct contact with affected cattle.

The balance of the $800,825 was spent tagging cattle in exposed herds and because of the enormous amount of money expended, statistics that are calculated to alarm the people are constantly being put in circulation.

Both the State Board of Health and the State Board of Agriculture are anxious that the State be relieved of any further trouble in the matter. The State authorities and the United States are not in accord as to the methods, and as the relations now stand they are only creative of confusion in the minds of the farmers and cattle owners. In 1878 Governor McClellan took up the matter of disease among animals, which was then quite prevalent all over the State, and appointed Gen. Sterling a member of his staff to look after the matter, and he expended $4,000 in his work, but was successful in getting rid of the plague excepting in Hudson county. In 1873, the quarantine against certain diseases including pleuro-pneumonia was transferred to the State Board of Health, and in 1883 the United States agreed to act in connection with the State. Only $5,900 per year is now allowed to be expended for pleuro-pneumonia, except when the Governor and Comptroller see fit to raise the amount to $5,000.

The State has the right to order and insist on quarantine for an afflicted herd. The United States makes inspection, polices the affected district and appraises the cattle in herd and kills them all whether they are affected or likely to be.

During the past year only $725 was spent by the State. In fact there is only $1,900 available for this purpose, because the act which allows the Director of the Experiment Station to condemn and burn cranberry vines affected with the fungus, allows the amount to be paid for damages to come from the pleuro-pneumonia fund to the extent of $1,600.

An attempt will be made to secure additional legislation on the subject of disease in cattle, particularly to more clearly define the purpose of the State, or else entirely relieve the State of the trouble.

LYNCHBURG, Sept. 25.—Special.
About $50 sporting men from Lynchburg, Roanoke and other points gathered at the Opera House tonight to witness a 10-round contest between Carter Lyons, the Roanoke lightweight champion of the South, and Jack Bolan, the Cincinnati lightweight. The fight was with 4-ounce gloves, bloomsbury rules, and was decided in favor of Bolan.

Lyons was seconded by Charles J. Ormsby and Bolan by C. J. Morarity. Promptly at 8:15 the principals entered the ring. When Referee Morris called time the men advanced to the center of the ring and shook hands.

The first round was characterized by good humor. Lyons pushed the fighting. In the second Lyons landed several good body blows and forced Bolan around the ring. Bolan landed on Lyons' neck.

The third and fourth were characterized by close in-fighting, in which Bolan had the best of it, landing telling blows on Lyons' body. In the fifth there was sharp sparring on both sides. Lyons landed right on Bolan's neck and the men clinched. The sixth and seventh were dull and embarrassing, with no blows of importance on either side. In the ninth there was very sharp in-fighting in Bolan's favor. Lyons' second claimed foul, but it did not go. Lyons knocked Bolan against the ropes by a powerful left-hander.

Both men came up in the tenth looking determined and this was the best round. Lyons led off with a hard blow just above the belt and forced Bolan to the rope. Bolan landed a hard one on Lyons' face and neck, the men clinched and broke away, sharp in-fighting following. Referee Morris then called time, advanced to the front and announced Bolan the winner. This was received with applause by the audience, who were clearly in sympathy with Bolan.

Lyons said he was not satisfied with the result, and would fight Bolan at any time for $500 if it could be done where the police would not interfere. Bolan was in good condition, but Lyons had not been in training.

with it. I was perplexed and wavered, the
slowly gathered fog, and the
chill of coming rain smote me through and
through, while in the distance there was the
roll of thunder.


It was now quite dark, very dark at that,
though at short intervals close to the bottom
faint gleams showed too dimly to
cast brightness of my path and only suf-
ficed to intensify the blackness about me.


All at once I saw a man walking should
join feet in front of me. Yes, I knew
it was already dark, but it was the same
person. He was walking in front
of me, and, with that more, could see that he
was a large man, dressed in rough clothes, well
dressed, although he wore heavy red
beard, and hat, and he looked back at me from
time to time with an expression of keen
anxiety on his otherwise relaxed features.


"Hello!" I cried, but as he did not halt
concluded he did not hear me. As second
call produced no result spurred my weary
horse up to overtake the stranger. But
though the gray responded with an effort,
most commendable under the circumstances,
I soon found that this strange pedestrian
did not intend to let me catch up with him.
Not that he hurried himself. He seemed
without an exertion to keep good feet in
feet between us.


Then I began to wonder how. With the
intense darkness shutting me in four
black walls, I was yet able to see my strange
companion so clearly, to take in the details
of his dress, and even the expression of his
face, and at that distance more than twice
my horse's length, when I could hardly see
his head before me. I am not given to great
superstitious fancies, and my only feeling was
one of curiosity.


We went on in silence for nearly half an
hour, when as suddenly as he had appeared
he was gone. I looked around for him,
half afraid, from his instant and complete
disappearance, that I had been dreaming.
Then I perceived that I was close to
a small, low building of some sort. Reined
in and shouted several times, but not the
slightest response could I hear, and at last
I rode boldly up and tapped on the wall
with the butt of my riding whip. Then, as
this elicited no sign of life, I concluded that
I had stumbled on some deserted house or
that it was the abode of my eccentric friend;
dismounting, tying the gray, I re-
solved to spend the rest of the night under
roof or to find some good reason for con-
tinuing my journey.


I felt my way along the wall until I reached
the door, and trying this end finding that it
yielded to me, stepped inside, striking
matches as I did &c. Fortunately, I carried
my matches in an airtight case, and as it was
dry the one struck gave me light at once.
I found myself in a large room close to
a fireplace, over which a rude shelf was placed,
and on this mantel I saw an oil lamp to
which I applied my match.


At the hearth was heaped a quantity of
ashes, and over the crouched child, a
girl of 6. At the end of the room
which was plainly and scantily furnished,
I lay man across a bed, and as I raised the
lamp I saw that he was the same man I had been
following, but there was something in a
throat and face that struck me as peculiar,
and was about to go forward and look at
him when the child, who had at first seemed
dazed at the light, fairly threw herself upon me.


"Have you anything for Nelly to eat?"
she said, and then, "Oh, Nelly so hungry!"


I ran my hand into my pocket and drew
out what had been a paper bag of choc-
olate candy, but was now pulp, unappetiz-
ing mass. I must confess to a childish
fondness for sweets, which I usually carry
to some form about me. I handed the re-
mains of my day's supply to the child and
then walked over to the bed. Yes, it was
the same man, red beard, rough clothes, but
setting of the magnificent frame to perish.
Not the same man, but dead, long dead.


I took his hand only to find it stiff and
cold, while his face had the dull gray aspect
never seen in the newly dead. As I stood
there, looking down on him, a little hand touched
mine.


"Nelly so hungry!" said the child.


"Have you eaten all the candy?" I asked
her.


"Yes, yes. But I am hungry, for I had
no dinner, no breakfast, no supper, and papa
won't get up."


The house, which consisted of the large
room, smaller kitchen and shed, where
I found a quantity of hay and fodder, seemed
quite bare of food, but by dint of search in
the hay I discovered a nest, which Nelly
informed me was there, and in it two fresh
eggs. These I boiled for her. When she
had finished, I soothed her to sleep on the bed
I made for her before the fire. Then, after
I had put my horse in the shed room and fed
him, I performed as well as I could service.

Duval, the young man who distinguished himself recently by naming a fictitious brood of young Duvals after various senators and representatives in Congress, securing many presents, pleaded guilty in the criminal court to three cases of false pretenses, and was sentenced to three years in the penitentiary in each case.

The ancient spirit is not dead. Old times, indeed, are speaking in the lines of the above paragraph. The Baltimorean Duval is genius, in his way, worthy of his namesake, the greater Claude of that name. But this particular Duval worked a smoother game. Claude's methods of obtaining filthy lucre were more dangerous to life and limb. He was the gentlemanly highwayman whose modus operandi was to politely ask travellers to stand and deliver, and if they were at all undecided what to do in the premises, they were soon persuaded that the best course was to accede to the peremptory demands of the robber.

But highway robbers are, comparatively speaking, relics of the past, and other methods have been invented less harsh and altogether more fastidious than in the ancient vulgar days. This bearer of the ancient name of Duval was an artist, so to speak, in his business. His methods were original in design and real in the manner of execution. His prey was, also, fat, sleek and easy, for perhaps there is nothing more gullible cast in nature's mould than the average congressman. He has a vanity to be tickled, a name to be handed down to posterity, which, perchance, will live to tell of statesmanlike acts and noble deeds which he himself could not accomplish, long after he has joined the great majority.

Some mute inglorious Jeremiah Simpson Smith, for instance, may bear silent, because unspeakable, testimony of the sockless statesman of Kansas long after the latter has been gathered to his fathers. Some Grover Cleveland Jackson yet unborn, may have his forename emblazoned with deeds of glory, the very sound of which will keep alive and lend an added halo to the memory of the fat free trade apostle.

Therefore, who can blame the illustrious congressmen and senators who quickly responded to Monsieur Duval's request, for a sum of money, because the child had been named after him. Duval was prolific, congressmen were gullible, and children multiplied fast indeed. And so, as very quickly little Duvals entered the cold, cold world, their putative parents as quickly named them after the members of the nation's folk, who were duly notified of the honor conferred, and who were more than willing to pay for it. Did not Duval know that the lamb is supposed to be tempered to be shorn, and were there no lambs to be shorn in Washington, and did not shivering little Duvals exist in his fertile imagination, who requires their fleeces wherewithal that they might be clothed?

Alas for human frailty, human duplicity and human gullibility! Duval will beget no more children with such wonderful rapidity for some time to come. The cold hand of the law was laid upon him, and another honest industry has been crushed through too much free trading upon the vanity of the wise men of the nation.

Duval will spend nine years behind prison bars, and some other knave will dupe the assembled wisdom in the nation's capital.

The law should deal very leniently with a crime like that of which he has been convicted, for is not Congress everybody's prey?
