Editor Herald:

Owing to certain events which have recently transpired in the 10th district in regard to consolidating the Public Schools, and being one of the School Directors of this district, I feel it has become my duty to ventilate the record of all individuals whom the people have entrusted and honored with the Office of School Director. I refer to T. G. Witherspoon, and I refer to him because he has prostituted the trust reposed in him in order to crafty his own selfish purposes, and against the wishes of the best people of this community.

In defining the character of this man whose "braying" has long since put to shame that of his four legged brother, it shall be my purpose to present the truth of the case, with ample evidence to corroborate all this article may contain.

Some time last fall the people of Goodwin and Knob Creek met for the purpose of combining the three schools of Goodwin, Phillip and Timmons. After much parleying the case was left to the directors. We selected a site, the house was put in repairs for the purpose of running a school. Then the question arose, who should be teachers. Green Witherspoon, in all the meetings which were held, had discoursed at length upon the necessity of procuring teachers who would be capable of building up a school, which in after years would be the pride and boast of the community. He was always cautious to repeat, in seeming sincerity; "Let us make no mistake in this matter; let us have teachers who will be the choice of the people and then all will be harmonic and success will be assured."

By common consent Prof. A. G. Allen, who is a gentleman of the highest honor and integrity and a thorough scholar, was chosen without dissenting voice in the district, to be the principal of the school.

Mr. H. S. Williams then applied for the place of assistant teacher; and I will state here that between Mr. Williams and myself there has always existed a warm friendship; but from objections that came to me every day from all quarters, I soon learned that it would be a step in the wrong direction in the community to employ him. And in a conversation with Witherspoon I told him that personally I would do anything in my power for Mr. Williams' success, but thought it best to procure some one who would suit the people. Mr. Witherspoon remarked to me that while he, (Williams) was a man of ability, there were serious objections to having the place, and that it would not do to put him in, and that under the circumstances he would not give his consent to Mr. Williams having the school. Soon after this it was rumored that Witherspoon was bringing to his aid his old tricks, &c., acquired years ago, of "Wire Working" and that Witherspoon was heard to say: "The time had come to take the bull by the horns" and he would put Williams in and keep him there the next two years, and if the people wanted to "kick" they could do so.

I gave the rumor little credit until I saw in his article in the Democrat that he had given the plum to Williams.

I then tried repeatedly to see Witherspoon and learn his reasons for trampling upon the rights of the people, but failed.

This is only one of the many instances which can be cited in his past history, where he has betrayed the people to accomplish his own selfish ends. He has long been known on Knob Creek as a subtle schemer, and it is conceded by his own neighbors and friends that whatever cause he advocates suffers from his being connected with it, and while apparently devoting all his ingenuities, and energies, in subscribing the interests of that cause, he is only waiting for a chance to take the "bull by the horns." He cares little for principles when there is an object to be attained, and has never hesitated to do violence to his conscience if he ever had a cause to attain the object in view.

When the SWISS delegation came in with its

ave do not expect that every kind OF labor

FOR SUNDAY OBSERVANCE.

Rev. DR. Edward Thompson's Address
at the First Methodist Church.

Rev. Edward Thompson, L.L.D., secretary for
the Pacific coast of the American Sabbath
Union, gave most interesting lecture last even-
ing in the First Methodist Episcopal church,
Marion and Third streets. His subject was,
"The Relation of the Sunday Movement to
Labor."

DR. Thompson took for his text, PHILIPPIANS,
"Look not every man on his own things,
but every man also on the things of Others."

"The most notable gathering that occurred in
Europe last year," he said, was the labor con-
gress called by Emperor William. There were
sixteen of the powers of Europe represented.
When the SWISS delegation came in with its
propositions, the first on the list was the Sunday
question, for they said the greatest thing for the
laborer was the protection of his weekly rest.
Thus this great matter was precipitated upon
the assembly and received most thorough dis-
cussion. As a result the matter was brought
into legislative assemblies in Germany, Austria,
France, Switzerland, Hungary and Belgium, and
in all some improvement was made in exist-
ing legislation, and almost exclusively from the
consideration of humanitarian which urge TO-
night final action has not yet been taken by
the French legislative corps, but all the other
national assemblies have acted. Only a few

weeks ago the German reichstag passed its bill,

which grants a Sunday rest to nearly all the la-
borers of Germany, and nowhere in the realm
of King William can man be discharged for re-
fusing TO do Sunday work.

In the last three years this question has been
coming to the front in the United States. The
greed of capital, the apathy of protesting Christ-
ians and the neglect of labor to assert its rights,
has making continued inroads upon the right to
sunday rest. This right is conceded in the
constitution of the United States, where the
president is guaranteed his Sunday rest. It is
conceded in the laws relating to the courts, leg-
islative assemblies and various departments of
government. It is conceded in the common
commercial laws of the country regulating
banks and wholesale establishments. Under
the principle of equal rights to all, which is the
fundamental law of the land, we claim for the
laborer the same privileges that are now granted
to these favored classes.

We do not expect that every kind of labor
can be stopped on Sunday, but we want to re-
duce that labor to the minimum, and whenever
man is obliged, from the necessities of his po-
sition, to work on Sunday, he must be granted
rest of an equal number of hours on some other
day of the week, without any reduction in his
monthly wages. This we claim as a law of hu-
manity—a law of equal rights.

"All the various classes of business should be
placed upon an equality. The man who clings
to the church and keeps a store ought to have an
equal chance with every other merchant in the
city. But your laws guarantee religious liberty
and under that pledge of your constitution he
closes his store on Sunday in obedience to law.
The man who keeps open his business house,
whether it be saloon or anything else, seven
days in the week gets an advantage over this
man in point of trade. There are very few lines
of business that are in any sense required to
keep open on Sunday, and the law makes wise
economists of the world have shown that all the
business of the week can be done in six or five
and one-half days instead of seven.

"Secondly, this is not only law of equa-
l rights, but law of health."

Dr. Thompson here exhibited diagram which
had been prepared by DR. Haegler, the eminent
scientist of Germany, by which he showed the
results of an experiment with six men who
worked six days in the week and six men who
worked seven days in the week, and it was
proved by this great scientist that the six-day
workers under the system of Sunday rest were
just as strong at the close of the month as they
were at the beginning; while the seven-day
workers lost steadily in nervous and physical
power from the first week.

Continuing he said no customs should be
permitted to exist in society which injure man
in his physical nature and are sure to break him
down before his natural time of decay.

"Third—This is a law of efficiency. Statistics

countries show that, other things being equal,
the men working under a six-day system do
more work in year, and a better average class
of work, than those who work under the seven
day system. As a notable example we would
compare the manufactures of England with
those of France. A certain prominent French
manufacturer, who made study of the ques-
tion last year, announced at the opening of 1891
that his establishment would thereafter run on
the six-day system. And his decision was
based purely upon monetary considerations.

"It is in the interest of labor to have this same
day rest, because the statistics of the world
show that, other things being equal, the laborer
gets the same wages per year under the six-day
principle as under the seven, thus receiving a
higher compensation for the number of hours
in which he is engaged. And besides he gets one
day each week for self-improvement.

home. We want to keep in this country a land
of homes. We want to retain the home day,
when the father is home from work and the
children are home from school, and all can put
on their best clothes and sing their songs and
enjoy a day of love and happiness together.

land of ours, where every man is a sovereign
charged with immense responsibility, every
man must be a thinker. He must have time to
think. One day each week should be set apart
to lofty thought, when the man can study
the great problems of today and make
himself worthy of American citizenship.

crime. Well regulated governments provide

the same percentage. The very first SUNDAY af-

cent the number of sunday arrest, which
for the year past had averaged 100, was reduced

"We trust that the laborers of this city will
join most heartily in this campaign. It is
truly for the best interests of all. For the sake
of our boys, to gain better character and
more intelligence to our voters, for the moral
elevation of the people, let us develop such a
sentiment in this noble city that the law
of Washington shall work into beautiful operation

pulp factory will follow immediately.

founding of a first class school at Big
Stone Gap, and are willing to help if the
company is properly organized. Professor
Bedford seems to be deeply interested in
getting up and carrying on a good school
at Big Stone Gap and we expect to con-
meet him with this enterprise at East Big
Stone Gap.

turned out over 100,000 feet of lumber
during the past winter. There are several
parties who have contracted recently to
build houses at East Big Stone Gap, and
expect to build one there myself. In fact
considering the short time we have been
at work, much progress has been made.

have begun building.

plants, and due credit will be given for

will be located on the Central Land Company
tract, near the L. & N. freight depot,
the company having given two acres of land
for this purpose.

Berryman, H. H. Bullitt and W. Z. Harris
mean by building those handsome resi-
dences on Poplar Hill?" All we can say is,

this summer."

caught the spirit of the building boom.

money. Rents are high, and houses in
great demand.

brick plant yesterday. He will be in full
blast in few days, with good force of
men.

home of John Powers, 1401 West Locust

inquest on the remains of Mrs. Powers
who had died suddenly the preceding day,
he found a shocking state of things,
which the Democrat describes as follows:

As well as could be learned from the
family, Mrs. Powers laid herself down
upon her bed Monday afternoon. It was
supposed she was asleep till some one
in the household went to rouse her, when it
was found that she was dead.

Tuesday, out of the remaining family
of four persons—the aged husband, the
son and the daughter of the deceased, and
the son's wife—the latter alone was sober.
The others were all deeply intoxicated.
The son was maudlin, and when told to
stop calling his wife a liar as she was
making her statement, he burst into tears
in foolish fear that some terrible thing
would be done to him. The husband was
not much better, and the daughter-in-law
alone was able to tell a story of what had
happened.

Powers was intoxicated, and that the son
went to a neighboring saloon for liquor
for her. While he was gone her death
occurred. It is the opinion of Dr. McCortney that she died for the want of the

accustomed to. She has been an habitual
drinker, in common with the other
members of the family, and the end that
came to her was astonishingly delayed.
She was 50 years of age. The family
came to Davenport from Ireland in 1855.

have in nearly every instance limited official
terms, never, however, destroying eligibility
for Office by reason of former service The

number is complete, of thirty-three members
who hold Office for life. All vacancies are
filled by the survivors. The officers of the
Supreme Council are also selected for life

members are selected as far as possible from
the several States comprising the jurisdiction,
without reference to the number of the
subordinate bodies or membership in such
state The object is to have one member
from each State. The Grand Commander,
Albert Pike, 33d degree, having died last
April, Mr., Bachelor, of New Orleans, who is
the Lieutenant Grand Commander, became at
once, under their laws, acting Grand Com
mander. He will SO continue until the next
meeting Of the Supreme Council, which will
be held in this city in October, 1892 at that
time the successor of Albert Pike will be
elected, more than probable for a short term
Of years, as the sentiment of the members
appears To be setting strongly in favor of a
representative form of government and the
abolition Of the life tenure of Office.

ust. If there were not money in the

he compiled an English-Hawaiian Die
ctionary, which is an invaluable work,
and shows how conversant he was with
the Hawaiian language. His memory
will be kept in grateful remembrance by
the Hawaiians as one of their true,
unselfish benefactors.

Hitchcock was held at the Halle Church,
Rev. Desha officiating, on Sunday, June
7th. His remains were interred by the
side of his mother in the Halai cemetery.

From the news, we learn that
Deputy Sheriff Searle nailed an opium
transaction, between the captain of the
Hall and a Chinaman, of some forty
tins. Is this part of the opium brought
by that sealing schooner?

The Volcano keeps up its late fires, but
the old pit of Halemaumau fills up slow
ly, and it is quite deep below the edge
of the rim. The lumber for the new
Volcano House is gradually arriving on
the ground, and work on the buildings
will ere long be commenced. We hear
that the hauling of this lumber over the
Lee road has knocked the stuffing out of
it. Why don't the people on Kau-
ai petition the Minister of the Interior to open
the road to the Volcano, so that that
matter can be settled by the next Legis-
lature?

Dies bedeutet war für Herbert von Horau eine traurige Gedanken, als er nach neuen Sorgen den Geist gesenkt und kein Haus einmal und traurig geworden war. Er hatte &c. glaubt, daß Glück und Lebensfreude für ihn mit ihr seitwärts sei. Hatte es ihm absichtlich in einem Schmerz; heute aber fühlte er, daß er auf neues Hoffen durfte, daß sein Herz noch mehr als mit Liebe fortwärts. Die er Maraa glaubte, daß er liebte, daß das Gefühl, aus welchem er seine Lebensgebung hatte, &c. werden, liebte sie, deren er lieb noch kaum betrübt geworden, für die er persönlich nach einem Namen gesucht. Aber wie anders war es heute als vor Jahren! Lucie's Herz hatte ihm gesagt, etc. er es versteht; Maraa war die Seine, aber ihm ihre Liebe konnte er erst werden.

Er aber war für die bekehrten Menschen in Unvollkommenheit. War, so leistete sich, an Beständigkeit. Leistete Hausarbeit, was möglich war der anstrengendste, liebenswürdigste Mensch, nachdem, welcher sich heute ausfüllte das Interesse seiner jungen Frau gehören wollte.

Am Ende des Tages waren die Berufsstunden des Professors wieder in ferne Rechte; Aufgabenarbeiten erwarteten ihn, und Schreibarbeiten auf die Erledigung.
Nach dem Abend der Gedanken hatte er ein paar Stunden gearbeitet, und am Morgen durfte er in wenig Zeit für das Zusammenleben mit Maraa bestimmt bis die Gelegenheit im der bergane günstige Grundbruch vieler Stunden den ganzen Tag.

Als er ihr Tochter aufstand hatte und Mara die Hand zum Liebesgruß reichte, sagte er ihr: „Meiner lieben, dass sie sich in ihrem neuen Heim wohl einlesen möge und um dich Gott bitten zu können. Alles nach dem Geschmack und Segen gestalten möge.“

Die Lippen, er liebten den Nutzen seiner jungen Frau liebten dankbar an ihn auf. „Wie gut Du bist, Herbert!“ sprach sie dabei; „Könnte ich Dir das Leben doch auch erleichtern und erfreuen! Sage mir, wenn Du mir etwas helfen kannst; es ist mir gern, meine Pflicht zu erfüllen.“

[Name] schrieb ihr: „Liebe Mara, es ist so schön, daß Du Dein Glück hast, Mara,“ steuerte er. Der, daß er nicht länger bei Dir halten kann, um Dich in Dein Heim einzulassen!

An ein unter Schmerzen Wintern nicht ihren Morgenpause nach, bevor die junge Frau in ihrer Ruhe ruhen musste. Die Abbru kam, in die Gesichter der geborenen Frau, zu empfangen, wie das verhieß, Mara mit die Wirklichkeit, Glück bis bald, ihr Leben, hier unterwegs. Die Schwierigkeiten waren - nicht nur Liebe, sondern auch Schmerz, und Unbehagen, daß C. Gil [Name] war, hier zu müssen. Witt einer &c. willen heute sie darauf in der Herbert's Zimmer, die, einfach und bequem, eine wirre Stätte seiner Arbeit war. Zu den Geschäftszimmern gab es ebenso als sie behaupten, denn der Professor hatte gute Entscheidungen und hatte sein Haus reich mit denselben ausgestattet. Sie ging auf gutem Wege von dem einen zum anderen, also sie wusste, daß er bei ihr gewesen ist, um sie zu belehren und ihr Gepräge zu teilen.

Aus erfüllt von dem Schmerz kam Mara wieder in ihrem Wohnzimmer an, dem trauligen Glanz, das Herbert's Hand ihr seitmäßig hatte. Sie betrachtete alles mit fröhlich frohem Blick, den weichen Zeppich, die herrlichen Teppichmuster, die kostbaren Blumen, Sie liebte es, einen der niederlieger zu sein und blickte mit traubendem Nase um sich, das alles kein Spiel ihrer, Barmherzigkeit, kein Grauen, der die einen einen Augenblick umdeckelt und dann sicherlich, die heute fortan in vielen Jahren, ihnen immer leben, pure Freundschaft und Liebe umsetzen; muß, sie nicht glücklich sein!

Und dies gab es Herbert's Freundschaft zu danken; was konnte er, ihm dabei sehen? Seine Freundschaft:

Was konnte sie ein Mann von kleinem Bedeutens, von seinem hohen Stand sein.

Was hatte er getrieben, gerade die unter vielen Spielen. Er konnte, zu er schaffen? Sie wusste es ja; ihre Zeit für sein Kind hatte er anfangen und nun trug sie ihren Sinn an sich.
